doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Drum solos and Mel Lewis on trading fours
summary: He treats drum solos like horn solos, cites Max Roach, and tells Mel Lewis's 'drummers' rights' story.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Has a drummer ever told you to just not play? Because that’s what happens a lot of times, you know the old joke about everybody starts talking during the bass solo, I think it’s partly because everybody else drops out.
Well I don’t drop out unless the bass player asks me to.

No, I might go to brushes just for the dynamic difference, or I just might play sticks softly, but I do, just like Rufus said, treat it like a horn solo. But people, everybody else stops when the drum takes his solo. That’s what kills me.

Yeah. Except, you know and Max Roach tried to change that a bit because the bass player would continue walking the changes of the tune on some of those recordings and Max would play over that, which is like saying hey, you know, I get a bass line too. But the majority of drum solos, I mean that’s a chance for the guys to go to the bar. So when I have my group, my little groups that I put together down here, I’ll tell the rest of the band, “Play behind me the same way you play behind a horn solo.” And I say to the horn player, “You can comp, comp on your horn.” And it’s not the usual way but at my age you don’t want to do things the usual way. And when you’re playing predominantly with young people, which is what I do, I do very little playing with my own age group you know, they’re open for anything. So it’s fun and they — that’s just sort of a side story about how drummers are treated. I’ll tell you one funny story: Mel Lewis, God rest his soul, I went to hear him play with some really good horn players in Connecticut where I was living at the time. And he’s laying time down behind these people, just I mean a dead man could swing it sounded so good. And then it came time to trade fours and eights and Mel did some things man that, you could see the horn players [counts] and their eyes getting big and when they came in it was all staggered. And Mel did this through the whole sequence. It was the last tune of the set, the finish. I go up to say hello to Mel and he’s surrounded by the horn players. They’re all bitching at him, “Mel, what the hell are you playing on your fours and eights. I couldn’t tell the time.” And Mel looked at them and said, “Look man, I sit up there and spend the majority of my time going ding-ding-a- ding-ding-a-ding behind your solos, so when it comes time for my solo I can play whatever in the hell I want to play. Case closed. Yeah, drummers’ rights.
